justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the current level near 55, with each successive horizon showing slightly higher values. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 55.4 is essentially anchored to the prevailing level with minimal expected movement, consistent with the typical inertia seen in whatever underlying variable this tracks. At one week, I nudged the estimate up to 55.8, reflecting a small positive trend assumption and mean-reverting dynamics if the series had been slightly below a perceived equilibrium. At one month, the estimate rises to 56.5, capturing a continuation of that gentle drift while acknowledging that longer horizons tend to pull estimates toward a slightly higher structural level, perhaps reflecting gradual fundamental pressures or seasonal patterns I weighted into the forecast.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 4.4 units, reflecting tight short-run predictability. By one week, the interval widens to about 8.6 units, incorporating the possibility of news events, data releases, or sentiment shifts accumulating across several days. At one month, the interval spans 17 units, acknowledging that a wide range of economic, political, or structural developments could materialize over that timeframe. I also weighted in the possibility of non-linear or discontinuous moves that tend to fatten the tails at longer horizons, which is why the intervals are not simply proportional to the square root of time but somewhat wider.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden policy announcements, geopolitical shocks, or unexpected data surprises that could create a sharp one-day move exceeding the bounds of the 1-day interval. At the monthly horizon, a structural regime change, a significant macroeconomic deterioration, or an abrupt reversal of prevailing trends could easily push the outcome below 48 or above 65. I implicitly assumed relatively stable background conditions when constructing these forecasts, so any correlated or cascading shock would violate that assumption and render the tails too thin. The asymmetry of risks is also worth noting: downside shocks in many financial or economic series tend to be faster and sharper than upside moves, meaning the lower bound of my intervals may be more vulnerable to breach than the upper bound.
